parts.prompt: Sum of two dice, given one die shows 6?

problems.title: Width
problems.statement: Rank these situations from tightest to widest market.

options: the counterparty has seen one of the dice
the distribution is fully known to both
you've seen one of the dice

problems.solution: An informed counterparty is the strongest reason to widen.

problems.title: Skew
problems.statement: You quote 6.8 / 7.2 on two dice and get lifted three times (sold 30 contracts at 7.2).

parts.prompt: Expected profit so far ($, 0.2 per contract)?

problems.solution: No new information about the dice, but a 30-lot short is risk; skew up to attract sellers.

problems.title: Expected P&L of a quote
problems.statement: Fair value 31.5, you quote 29.5 / 33.5; a noise trader buys or sells with ½ each.
problems.solution: Buy at 33.5 or sell at 29.5, each 2 better than fair.

problems.title: Updating
problems.statement: The hidden value is the sum of three uniform 1–20 draws. Revealed: 17.

parts.prompt: SD of the remaining two draws' sum (√(2 × (20² − 1)/12))?

problems.solution: 38; SD ≈ 8.15, so a sensible width is a few points either side.

problems.title: Crossed

options: anyone buys at 9 and sells at 10 for a riskless 1

problems.solution: A crossed market is an arbitrage against you.

problems.title: Sizing the width
problems.statement: Fair value 50 with a standard deviation of uncertainty 4; you want an informed counterparty to profit only rarely.

problems.title: Figgie-style inference
problems.statement: A deck has 12 cards of a goal suit and 10 of others; you hold 4 of the suit in a 10-card hand drawn from a 40-card deck where the suits are 12, 10, 10, 8.

parts.prompt: Your expected count of a 12-card suit in a random 10-card hand?
Holding 4 of a suit (above 3 expected) makes it…
options: more likely to be the 12-card suit

hints: Likelihoods of your hand under each hypothesis.
problems.solution: 3 expected; holding more is evidence for the larger suit (Bayes, Part 13.2).
